mean: to speak bluntly, without mincing words
lit: to speak straight out, avoiding no taboo subject

use.how: Adverbial (直言不讳地指出) or predicate. Said of someone who openly states criticism or an unwelcome truth.

near.diff: 心直口快 is a personality that blurts out whatever it thinks; 直言不讳 is openly stating an unwelcome truth on a given occasion.

cue: Everyone at the meeting praised the plan, but one engineer stood up and said plainly that it would fail. How did she speak?

ctx.s: 朋友{直言不讳}地告诉我，这件衣服不适合我。
ctx.en: My friend told me straight out that this outfit doesn't suit me.

ctx.s: 会上，她{直言不讳}地指出了方案里的三个问题。
ctx.en: At the meeting she bluntly pointed out three problems in the plan.

ctx.s: 你觉得我的论文怎么样？请{直言不讳}，不用客气。
ctx.en: What do you think of my thesis? Please be blunt, don't be polite.

ctx.s: 这位评论家一向{直言不讳}，很多导演都怕他。
ctx.en: This critic has always been outspoken, and many directors are afraid of him.

ctx.s: 面对记者的提问，部长{直言不讳}地承认了工作中的失误。
ctx.en: Faced with the reporters' questions, the minister frankly admitted the mistakes that had been made.

ctx.s: 他在信中{直言不讳}，把公司管理上的问题一条条列了出来。
ctx.en: In his letter he held nothing back, listing the company's management problems one by one.

bad.s: 他{直言不讳}地走进了办公室。
bad.en: (meant: he walked straight into the office)
bad.why: The 'straight' here is about speech, not direction; the idiom only describes how someone speaks.

bad.s: 他不想让别人知道这件事，所以{直言不讳}。
bad.en: (meant: he didn't want anyone to know, so he kept quiet)
bad.why: The idiom means speaking openly and holding nothing back, the opposite of keeping quiet.

mean: to advise someone earnestly and patiently
lit: a toiling mouth and a grandmother's heart: urging again and again with an old woman's kindly care

use.how: Adverbial before 劝/说/叮嘱 (苦口婆心地劝他) or predicate. Stresses patient, repeated urging meant to make someone change.

near.diff: 语重心长 describes the weight and sincerity of what is said in one talk; 苦口婆心 stresses urging patiently, again and again.

cue: For a whole month a mother kept patiently reasoning with her son, day after day, to get him to stop gaming all night. How did she advise him?

ctx.s: 妈妈{苦口婆心}地劝他少玩游戏，他就是不听。
ctx.en: His mother kept patiently urging him to play fewer games, but he just wouldn't listen.

ctx.s: 老师{苦口婆心}说了半天，他终于答应回学校上课了。
ctx.en: After the teacher had reasoned with him at length, he finally agreed to come back to class.

ctx.s: 我{苦口婆心}劝了你多少次，你怎么还是不戴头盔？
ctx.en: How many times have I begged you, and you still don't wear a helmet?

ctx.s: 医生{苦口婆心}地劝了好几回，老人才答应戒酒。
ctx.en: Only after the doctor had patiently urged him several times did the old man agree to give up drinking.

ctx.s: 不管社区工作人员怎么{苦口婆心}地劝，那家人还是不肯搬走。
ctx.en: No matter how patiently the community workers pleaded, that family still refused to move out.

ctx.s: 经过朋友们一次又一次{苦口婆心}的劝说，他总算把烟戒了。
ctx.en: After his friends had patiently reasoned with him time and again, he finally quit smoking.

bad.s: 这个药{苦口婆心}，但是效果很好。
bad.en: (meant: this medicine tastes bitter but works well)
bad.why: The 'mouth' part means painstaking, earnest words, not a bitter taste; the idiom describes a person giving advice, never medicine or food.

bad.s: 他{苦口婆心}地骂了我一顿，让我马上滚出去。
bad.en: (meant: he gave me a harsh telling-off and told me to get out)
bad.why: It implies patient, caring persuasion; an angry scolding that drives someone away is the opposite.

lit: the words are heavy and the heart is long: weighty words from a deeply caring heart

use.how: Adverbial before 说/叮嘱 (语重心长地说) or attributive (语重心长的话). Usually an elder or superior speaking earnestly to someone younger.

near.diff: 苦口婆心 stresses patient, repeated persuasion; 语重心长 stresses how weighty and heartfelt the words are, even if said only once.

cue: Before his grandson left for university, the old man took him aside and said a few solemn, heartfelt words about how to live. How did he speak?

ctx.s: 爷爷{语重心长}地对我说：“做人要诚实。”
ctx.en: Grandpa said to me earnestly, "You must be an honest person."

ctx.s: 毕业那天，校长{语重心长}地叮嘱我们不要忘记初心。
ctx.en: On graduation day the principal earnestly urged us never to forget why we started.

ctx.s: 父亲那番{语重心长}的话，我到现在还记得。
ctx.en: I still remember those heartfelt words of advice from my father.

ctx.s: 老教授拍拍他的肩膀，{语重心长}地说：“年轻人，别着急。”
ctx.en: The old professor patted his shoulder and said earnestly, "Young man, don't be in a hurry."

ctx.s: 这封信写得{语重心长}，字里行间都是对学生的关心。
ctx.en: The letter was written with deep sincerity; every line showed care for the students.

ctx.s: 他本以为会挨批评，没想到经理只是{语重心长}地提醒他注意身体。
ctx.en: He expected a telling-off, but the manager just earnestly reminded him to look after his health.

bad.s: 他{语重心长}地讲了个笑话，大家都笑了。
bad.en: (meant: he told a joke and everyone laughed)
bad.why: It describes solemn, earnest advice; it cannot describe telling a joke.

bad.s: 这个箱子太{语重心长}了，我搬不动。
bad.en: (meant: this box is too heavy for me to carry)
bad.why: The 'heavy' refers to the weight of words, not physical weight; the idiom only describes speech.

lit: heard on the road, passed on along the way

story.text: Confucius said that to hear something on the road and repeat it further along the way is to throw away virtue: passing on what you have picked up by chance, without checking it, is a moral failing and not just a careless habit.

use.how: Predicate, attributive (道听途说的消息) or after 是/靠. Dismisses information as unverified, second-hand talk.

near.diff: 捕风捉影 is making claims or accusations on no basis at all; 道听途说 is information picked up second-hand and repeated unchecked.

cue: Your neighbour says the factory is closing because someone at the market told her so. How would you describe her news?

ctx.s: 这些都是{道听途说}，你别当真。
ctx.en: That's all just hearsay, don't take it seriously.

ctx.s: 写新闻不能靠{道听途说}，一定要找到可靠的来源。
ctx.en: You can't write news based on hearsay; you must find a reliable source.

ctx.s: 你说他要辞职了？是真的，还是{道听途说}的？
ctx.en: You say he's resigning? Is that true, or just something you heard?

ctx.s: 网上很多{道听途说}的健康知识，其实没有科学根据。
ctx.en: A lot of second-hand health tips online have no scientific basis.

ctx.s: 他把{道听途说}的消息讲得跟亲眼看见一样。
ctx.en: He tells news he only heard about as if he had seen it with his own eyes.

ctx.s: 法官提醒证人，只陈述亲眼所见，不要说{道听途说}的内容。
ctx.en: The judge reminded the witness to state only what he saw himself, not things he had heard from others.

bad.s: 我昨天在路上{道听途说}，遇到了一个老同学。
bad.en: (meant: on the road yesterday I ran into an old classmate)
bad.why: The road is only an image; the idiom means unverified hearsay, not anything that happened on a road.

bad.s: 这是校长亲口宣布的{道听途说}，大家放心吧。
bad.en: (meant: this is news the principal announced in person, so relax)
bad.why: Something announced first-hand by the source is the opposite of hearsay, and the idiom is dismissive.

lit: to cut off one stanza and take a meaning from it

story.text: In the Zuo Zhuan, Lupu Gui of Qi married a woman of his own clan, which custom forbade. Asked why, he replied that when people recite the Book of Songs they cut out a single stanza and take from it only the meaning they want; he too had simply taken what he wanted. The idiom grew from his phrase about cutting off a stanza, and came to mean lifting words out of their context.

use.how: Predicate or adverbial (断章取义地引用). Criticises quoting a fragment so that it seems to say what the whole does not.

near.diff: 以偏概全 judges the whole from one part; 断章取义 distorts what someone said or wrote by lifting out a fragment.

cue: A newspaper printed only half of the minister's sentence, so it looked as if she had said the opposite of what she meant. What did the paper do?

ctx.s: 你只截取了我说的半句话，这是{断章取义}。
ctx.en: You've lifted just half of what I said; that's quoting me out of context.

ctx.s: 我的原话不是这个意思，请不要{断章取义}。
ctx.en: That's not what my original words meant; please don't quote me out of context.

ctx.s: 这段视频被人剪掉了前后内容，{断章取义}地传到了网上。
ctx.en: Someone cut what came before and after in this clip and posted it online out of context.

ctx.s: 读古书最怕{断章取义}，要把上下文一起看。
ctx.en: The worst thing when reading classical texts is to take lines out of context; you have to read what surrounds them.

ctx.s: 那家媒体{断章取义}，把专家的提醒写成了警告。
ctx.en: That outlet quoted the expert out of context, turning a reminder into a warning.

ctx.s: 他引用老师的话时{断章取义}，故意漏掉了后半句。
ctx.en: When he quoted the teacher he twisted her words, deliberately leaving out the second half of the sentence.

bad.s: 这篇文章太长了，我{断章取义}，只讲第一部分。
bad.en: (meant: the article is long, so I'll pick out just the first part to discuss)
bad.why: It is always a criticism of distorting meaning, never a neutral way of saying you are taking an excerpt.

bad.s: 老师让我们把课文{断章取义}，分成四段。
bad.en: (meant: the teacher had us divide the text into four sections)
bad.why: It has nothing to do with dividing a text into parts; it means misrepresenting words by quoting a fragment.

lit: to paint the sounds and paint the colours

use.how: Adverbial (绘声绘色地讲) or complement after 得 (讲得绘声绘色). Said of vivid storytelling, description or imitation.

near.diff: 栩栩如生 says a picture, carving or character looks alive; 绘声绘色 says someone tells or describes something vividly.

cue: Grandpa tells how he met a bear in the woods, imitating its roar and every movement, and the children hang on every word. How does he tell it?

ctx.s: 爷爷讲故事讲得{绘声绘色}，孩子们都听入迷了。
ctx.en: Grandpa tells stories so vividly that the children are spellbound.

ctx.s: 她{绘声绘色}地描述了旅行中遇到的趣事。
ctx.en: She gave a lively account of the funny things that happened on her trip.

ctx.s: 他在电话里把事故经过讲得{绘声绘色}，我听得心惊肉跳。
ctx.en: On the phone he described the accident so vividly that my heart was in my mouth.

ctx.s: 你说得这么{绘声绘色}，好像你当时就在现场似的。
ctx.en: You describe it so vividly, as if you had been there yourself.

ctx.s: 导游{绘声绘色}地讲起这座古城的传说，游客们都停下了脚步。
ctx.en: The guide began telling the legends of the old town so vividly that the tourists all stopped to listen.

ctx.s: 他{绘声绘色}地模仿老师上课的样子，全班哈哈大笑。
ctx.en: He did a lifelike impression of the teacher in class, and the whole class roared with laughter.

bad.s: 这幅画颜色很{绘声绘色}，挂在客厅很好看。
bad.en: (meant: this painting's colours are bright and it looks good in the living room)
bad.why: Despite 'painting colours' in its image, it describes vivid telling or describing, not the colours of a real painting.

bad.s: 他的嗓音很{绘声绘色}，很适合唱歌。
bad.en: (meant: he has a lovely voice, well suited to singing)
bad.why: It describes how vivid an account is, not the quality of someone's voice.

lit: to force words and seize the argument

use.how: Predicate (你这是强词夺理) or adverbial. Criticises someone who is in the wrong but argues anyway with twisted reasoning.

near.diff: 胡搅蛮缠 is pestering and making a scene with no reasoning at all; 强词夺理 puts on a show of argument to defend a weak position.

cue: Caught running a red light, a driver insists the light was only just red and the camera angle was unfair. What is he doing?

ctx.s: 明明是你错了，还{强词夺理}！
ctx.en: You're obviously in the wrong, and you're still arguing!

ctx.s: 他迟到了一个小时，却{强词夺理}，说是我们来得太早。
ctx.en: He was an hour late, yet he twisted things round and said we had come too early.

ctx.s: 你别{强词夺理}了，证据都在这儿。
ctx.en: Stop twisting the facts, the evidence is right here.

ctx.s: 孩子打碎了花瓶，还{强词夺理}地说是花瓶自己掉下去的。
ctx.en: The child broke the vase and still insisted it had fallen off by itself.

ctx.s: 面对质问，那位发言人只能{强词夺理}，越说越没人信。
ctx.en: Under questioning the spokesman could only argue lamely, and the more he said, the less anyone believed him.

ctx.s: 辩论要讲道理，靠{强词夺理}是赢不了评委的。
ctx.en: A debate is about reasoning; you won't win the judges over by twisting words.

bad.s: 他的论证{强词夺理}，证据充分，大家都被说服了。
bad.en: (meant: his argument was strong and well supported, and everyone was convinced)
bad.why: It is not praise for a 'strong' argument; the idiom accuses someone of arguing when they are in the wrong.

bad.s: 我们{强词夺理}地讨论了一下午，终于有了结论。
bad.en: (meant: we debated hard all afternoon and finally reached a conclusion)
bad.why: It is not a word for lively discussion; it accuses one person of twisting words to defend being wrong.

lit: those who come later end up on top

story.text: Ji An, a blunt minister of Emperor Wu of Han, saw men who had once ranked below him promoted over his head. He told the emperor: Your Majesty uses officials the way one stacks firewood, and the pieces that come later end up on top. In its origin it was a complaint; today it usually praises a latecomer that overtakes those who started earlier.

use.how: Predicate, said of a person, team, company or country that started late or fell behind and then pulled ahead: 他们后来居上，拿了冠军。

near.diff: 青出于蓝 is a student surpassing their own teacher; 后来居上 is any latecomer overtaking those who started earlier.

cue: A small startup launched years after the big firms, yet within three years it has more users than any of them. What happened?

ctx.s: 他上学期成绩一般，这学期{后来居上}，考了全班第一。
ctx.en: His grades were average last term, but this term he overtook everyone and came top of the class.

ctx.s: 比赛最后一圈，那位年轻选手{后来居上}，超过了所有人。
ctx.en: On the last lap the young runner came from behind and passed everyone.

ctx.s: 这家公司起步最晚，却{后来居上}，成了行业里的龙头。
ctx.en: This company started the latest, yet it overtook the rest and became the industry leader.

ctx.s: 别看我们现在落后，只要努力，完全可以{后来居上}。
ctx.en: We may be behind now, but if we work hard we can certainly overtake them.

ctx.s: 电动车市场竞争激烈，几个新品牌已经有{后来居上}之势。
ctx.en: The electric car market is fiercely competitive, and several new brands are already on course to overtake the old ones.

ctx.s: 他是最后一个加入团队的，没想到{后来居上}，第一个升了职。
ctx.en: He was the last to join the team, but surprisingly he got ahead of everyone and was the first promoted.

bad.s: 他每天都{后来居上}，总是最后一个到办公室。
bad.en: (meant: he's always the last to arrive at the office)
bad.why: It means overtaking those ahead, not simply arriving late.

bad.s: 我们队从头到尾一直领先，最后也是{后来居上}。
bad.en: (meant: our team led from start to finish and won)
bad.why: A team that led all along did not come from behind; the idiom needs a latecomer passing the leaders.

mean: first impressions take hold and colour later judgment
lit: what enters first becomes the master

use.how: Predicate, adverbial or attributive (先入为主的印象/观念). Said of an early impression or idea that biases later judgment, usually as a warning.

near.diff: 偏听偏信 is trusting only one side's account; 先入为主 is letting whatever you heard or thought first decide the matter.

cue: You read one bad review before seeing a film, and you dislike it even though the film itself is fine. What is shaping your opinion?

ctx.s: 第一次见面印象不好，我就{先入为主}地认为他不好相处。
ctx.en: Our first meeting went badly, so I assumed from then on that he was hard to get along with.

ctx.s: 看病的时候，医生不能{先入为主}，要把检查做完再下结论。
ctx.en: When treating a patient, a doctor mustn't go on first impressions, but should finish the tests before deciding.

ctx.s: 人们常有一种{先入为主}的观念，觉得贵的东西一定好。
ctx.en: People often have a preconceived idea that expensive things must be good.

ctx.s: 你是不是{先入为主}了？先听听他怎么解释吧。
ctx.en: Aren't you prejudging this? Hear his explanation first.

ctx.s: 审案时，法官必须避免{先入为主}，只看证据。
ctx.en: In hearing a case, a judge must avoid preconceptions and look only at the evidence.

ctx.s: 因为先看了电视剧，我{先入为主}，总觉得原著的主角就该是那个演员的样子。
ctx.en: Because I saw the TV series first, it's stuck with me: I always picture the novel's hero as that actor.

bad.s: 他每天都{先入为主}，第一个走进教室。
bad.en: (meant: every day he's the first to walk into the classroom)
bad.why: 'Entering first' is not about arriving somewhere; the idiom is about first impressions biasing judgment.

bad.s: 排队的时候要{先入为主}，后来的人等一等。
bad.en: (meant: in a queue it's first come, first served)
bad.why: First come, first served is a different phrase; this idiom describes a bias in judgment, not the order of a queue.

mean: to depend on each other to survive
lit: to lean on each other as one's very life

story.text: Li Mi, summoned to serve the Jin court, wrote to the emperor asking to be excused. Orphaned as a small child, he had been raised by his grandmother, now old and ill: without her he would not have lived to manhood, and without him she could not live out her years. Grandmother and grandson, he wrote, lived for each other. The idiom is traced to this line of the letter, though the wording there is slightly different.

use.how: Predicate, typically 两人相依为命 or 和…相依为命. Said of people, or a person and an animal, who have only each other, usually in hardship.

near.diff: 同甘共苦 is sharing good times and bad as partners; 相依为命 says each has only the other to live for.

cue: After the war took the rest of the family, an old woman and her little grandson were left with only each other. How did they live?

ctx.s: 父母去世后，姐弟俩{相依为命}。
ctx.en: After their parents died, the sister and brother had only each other.

ctx.s: 老人和他的狗{相依为命}，已经十几年了。
ctx.en: The old man and his dog have had only each other for more than ten years.

ctx.s: 那些年家里很穷，我和妈妈{相依为命}，日子过得很苦。
ctx.en: We were very poor in those years; my mother and I depended on each other, and life was hard.

ctx.s: 小说讲的是一对在战乱中{相依为命}的祖孙。
ctx.en: The novel is about a grandparent and grandchild who cling to each other through the chaos of war.

ctx.s: 你们母女{相依为命}这么多年，她舍不得你出国也很正常。
ctx.en: You and your mother have relied only on each other for so many years; it's natural she can't bear to let you go abroad.

ctx.s: 地震后，这两位失去家人的老人互相照顾，{相依为命}。
ctx.en: After the earthquake, the two old people who had lost their families looked after each other and lived for each other.

bad.s: 我和同事{相依为命}，一起完成了这个项目。
bad.en: (meant: my colleague and I worked closely together to finish the project)
bad.why: It means having only each other to survive hardship; it is far too heavy for ordinary teamwork.

bad.s: 这两家公司{相依为命}，签了合作合同。
bad.en: (meant: the two companies depend on each other and signed a cooperation agreement)
bad.why: It describes people, or a person and an animal, whose lives hang on each other, not business partners.
